Intel and Micron to start sampling memristor storage

I always thought HP would be first, but maybe they're spending too much time focusing on eliminating storage hierarchies (replace cache, DRAM, and disk with memristor-based storage).

Interestingly enough, this press release claims 1000x faster and 1000x higher endurance than NAND, but just higher density than DRAM, not faster speeds.

AFAIK, it was never intended to be faster than DRAM. It has big implications for power consumption in mobile electronics, where you can shut off the device instantly and resume later rather than keeping it in sleep mode. Also, it could be used to get rid of the distinction between RAM (short-term memory) and mass storage (long-term memory).
HP claimed last year they had memristors operating at 100picoseconds, fast enough to completely collapse the memory hierarchy, including replacement of the SRAM now used just as caches.

"For example, retailers may use 3D XPoint technology to more quickly identify fraud detection patterns in financial transactions"

Was that just plucked out of thin air? How would a retailer have access to a customers purchasing history if they were a new customer? This sounds all great but in real terms I don't see like this will be major break through, but an easier way to store long term data. In our datacentres, modern high performance systems have lightening fast disk access combined with obscene amounts of RAM. I doubt this technology will make it into the DC arena for a good few years yet.

For me it's processing speeds that still need to evolve. This will help, but won't be a major game changer any time soon.

This is pie in the sky, there's not facility for stores to share transaction data, and this is already done by your credit / debit card supplier. In the UK we have fraud protection that prevents irregular purchases without the need of this. Modern data processing systems can walk through your entire life time purchase history in a matter of seconds if that.....

Current storage is not too slow at all, being a data centre engineer, we run an ESX estate of 6 hosts running around 300 Citrix Xen desktops with an additional 700 high performance VMs (mixture of Windows servers and RedHat) and we don't touch the side on our storage, the IOPS never go above 10%, and this is only a SMB implementation. Storage platforms such as Nimble/HDS offer ridiculous through put (the HDS G1000 offers 896 GB/sec aggregate internal bandwidth of up to 12.3PB of storage).

I meant across multiple sites for a single chain. But thinking about it you're right, even a large chain would only have a few million transactions a day, even current technology should be fast enough for the fraud detection application they mentioned.

That's just marketing speak, but this is good news for anyone from datacenters and supercomputers and cell phone users.

It is almost the same philosophy behind the 10 core, 3 cluster chip from MediaTek. Having another storage "tier" means better efficiency in any device that can hold all three (DRAM, XPoint, and NAND). Except that this is a lot closer to DRAM than NAND, and it's non-volatile. While they say that this does not replace DRAM, it actually could in many cases. Datacenters keep some data on DRAM... now they can get double capacity for the same price in nonvolatile form. The latency isn't much worse than DRAM. It is 10x more compact than DRAM. If it is used as primary memory it could be used to create an instant-on device in any form: phone to server.

As the price falls it could seriously displace NAND and DRAM. NAND faces endurance problems, even with V-NAND. The fastest NAND with the most endurance is also the most expensive and least dense (SLC). Instead of an SLC cache in SSDs, this could be used instead. The small 32-64 GB SSDs that people use to store operating system and frequently used applications will be replaced by XPoint. The first XPoint products should be 16 GB. 16 GB could store most of Windows OS for less than $100 (pricing unknown), and it could fit a 3 GB phone OS and many applications. 32 GB fits the entire Windows OS and some applications. And so on. If the product is 2-3 times less expensive than each GB of DRAM and more dense than DRAM, it could be more useful to have a smaller amount of fast DDR4 or HBM memory and a 16-32 GB chunk of XPoint.
